'''Roger Elwood Batzel''' (December 1, 1921 – July 29, 2000) was an American [[Nuclear chemistry|nuclear scientist]], best known as the director of the [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]] for over sixteen years, from 1971 to 1988.<ref name="lllnlbyr">{{cite journal |last=Nuckolls |first=John H. |date=January–February 2001 |title=A career of distinguished achievement |url=https://www.llnl.gov/str/January01/Batzel1.html |journal=Science & Technology Review |accessdate=May 8, 2014}}</ref><ref name=nytobit>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/08/02/us/roger-batzel-nuclear-chemist-and-livermore-lab-director-78.html |newspaper=New York Times |last=Saxon |first=Wolfgang |title=Roger Batzel, nuclear chemist And Livermore Lab Director, 78 |date=August 2, 2000 |accessdate=May 8, 2014}}</ref><ref name=latimeobt>{{cite news|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2000-aug-03-me-63751-story.html |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |title=Roger Batzel; Livermore Lab Director for 17 Years |date=August 3, 2000 |access-date=May 8, 2014}}</ref>

==Early years==
Born and raised in [[Weiser, Idaho]], Batzel graduated from [[Weiser High School]] in 1940 and enrolled at the [[University of Idaho]] in Moscow.<ref name=lind41>{{cite web|url=http://issuu.com/uidahodigital/docs/gem1941/189 |publisher=Gem of the Mountains, University of Idaho yearbook |year=1941|title=Lindley Hall |page=185}}</ref><ref name=senr47>{{cite web|url=http://issuu.com/uidahodigital/docs/gem1947/52|publisher=Gem of the Mountains, University of Idaho yearbook |year=1947 |title=Seniors |page=52}}</ref> He left college during [[World War II]] to serve in the [[United States Army Air Forces|U.S. Army Air Forces]] as a [[Navigator Badge|navigation]] instructor, then returned to UI and earned a [[bachelor's degree]] in [[chemical engineering]] in 1947.<ref name=senr47/>

Batzel worked for [[General Electric]] for a year at nearby [[Hanford Site|Hanford]], [[Washington (state)|Washington]], then attended graduate school at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. He earned a [[Doctorate#United States|Ph.D.]] in nuclear chemistry in 1951, studying under Dr. [[Glenn T. Seaborg]], a [[List of Nobel laureates in Chemistry|Nobel Prize]] winner that same year.<ref name=nytobit/><ref name=latimeobt/> Batzel then worked as a senior chemist for California Research and Development Co.<ref name=asstspiv>{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=ithHAAAAIBAJ&pg=4777%2C546971 |newspaper=Victoria (TX) Advocate |title=Atomic scientist slated to speak in Victoria |date=March 27, 1960 |page=1}}</ref>

==Lawrence Livermore==
Batzel joined the University of California Radiation Laboratory at [[Livermore, California|Livermore]] in its second year in 1953 as an assistant division leader with the chemistry department, and became its head in 1959.<ref name=asstspiv/> (Shortly after [[Ernest Lawrence]]'s death in August 1958, the Berkeley and Livermore labs were renamed "Lawrence Radiation Laboratory.")

In 1961, Batzel became associate director of chemistry and was also named associate director of nuclear testing, a position he held until 1964.  He was associate director of chemistry and space reactors from 1966 to 1968 and associate director of chemistry and biomedical research in 1969.

Batzel was appointed as the newly renamed Lawrence Livermore Laboratory's sixth director on December 1, 1971, his 50th birthday.<ref name=lllnlbyr/> He was its longest-serving director and was one of the nation's leading authorities on [[nuclear weapon]]s,<ref name=fobinr>{{cite news |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1991/08/13/fire-on-bomber-in-1980-posed-nuclear-risk/ |newspaper=Chicago Tribune |last=Karaim |first=Reed |agency=Knight-Ridder Tribune News |title=Fire on bomber in 1980 posed nuclear risk |date=August 13, 1991 |access-date=May 8, 2014 }}</ref> advising four [[President of the United States|U.S. presidents]]. Under his guidance, the Laboratory broadened its mission from primarily nuclear weapons to many areas of applied science, and he stepped down in April 1988 at age 66.<ref name=lllnlbyr/><ref name=sfgtrb>{{cite news|url=http://www.sfgate.com/news/article/Roger-Batzel-2746261.php |publisher= SF Gate |title=Roger Batzel |date=August 1, 2000 |accessdate=May 8, 2014}}</ref>

==Death==
Batzel suffered a major [[Myocardial infarction|heart attack]] in July 2000 at age 78 and died several days later in a [[San Ramon, California|San Ramon]] hospital. Later that year, the Laboratory dedicated Building 132, the national security building, in Batzel's memory for his "legacy of excellence in support of national security."<ref name=lllnlbyr/>

==Personal==
Batzel was married to Edwina (Grindstaff) Batzel (b. 1926) for 54 years and they had three children, a son and two daughters.<ref name=nytobit/> He is buried at Queen of Heaven Cemetery in [[Lafayette, California|Lafayette]], California.<ref name=billgra>{{cite news|url=http://billiongraves.com/pages/record/ROGEREBATZEL/6246406 |publisher=Billion Graves |title=Roger Batzel |accessdate=May 8, 2014}}</ref>
